theme: Locusts, darkness, and the warning of the firstborn
readingInstruction: Read Exodus 10:1-11:10. These chapters contain the plagues of locusts and darkness, and the announcement of the last plague. Read them as the climax of the confrontation, and notice how Pharaoh’s bargaining shows what his heart is really protecting.
settingTheScene: Seven plagues have passed. Egypt is ruined: the Nile is blood, the land is covered in frogs, flies, and dead animals, and its crops have been shattered by hail. Pharaoh’s own officials say, “Do you not yet understand that Egypt is destroyed?” (10:7). Still he refuses. The last three plagues are the most terrible, and they lead up to the event that will define Israel’s identity for the rest of its history.
observation: God tells Moses to go to Pharaoh, “that I may show these signs of mine among them, and that you may tell in the hearing of your son and of your grandson how I have dealt harshly with the Egyptians” (10:1-2).
Pharaoh’s servants beg, “How long shall this man be a snare to us? Let the men go, that they may serve the LORD their God” (10:7).
Pharaoh bargains: only the men may go (10:11). The locusts eat everything that is left after the hail (10:12-15).
After the locusts, Pharaoh says, “I have sinned against the LORD your God, and against you” (10:16), and then hardens his heart again.
The ninth plague is “a darkness to be felt” that lasts three days, but “all the people of Israel had light where they lived” (10:21-23).
Pharaoh offers another bargain: the people may go, but their flocks and herds must stay. Moses answers, “Not a hoof shall be left behind” (10:24-26).
Pharaoh says, “Get away from me; take care never to see my face again” (10:28). Moses replies, “You have spoken rightly. I will not see your face again” (10:29).
God announces the last plague: “About midnight I will go out in the midst of Egypt, and every firstborn in the land of Egypt shall die” (11:4-5).
“Not a dog shall growl against any of the people of Israel…that you may know that the LORD makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel” (11:7).
interpretation:
Pharaoh’s bargains are worth studying, because people still bargain with God in the same ways. First he says, “Go and sacrifice here in the land.” That is, serve God, but on my terms and in my territory. Then he says, “Only the men may go.” That is, serve God, but leave your children and keep your families under my control. Then, “Go, but leave your flocks.” That is, serve God, but keep what you own under my power. Each time Moses refuses. “Not a hoof shall be left behind.” Everything belongs to God, and nothing can be held back.

The pattern is not about distant history. Many people want a version of faith that costs them nothing: Christianity at church but not at home, in the heart but not in the wallet, for the individual but not for the family. Moses’ answer is that God asks for the whole thing.

The plague of darkness is the strangest. It is described as a “darkness to be felt.” It was so thick that people did not see one another or rise from their places for three days. This is a reversal of the first day of creation, when God said, “Let there be light.” The land of Egypt is un-created. It is also a picture of what it means to live without God: a darkness that you can feel. And in Goshen, the people of God had light. That is a vivid image of the difference God makes.

Pharaoh’s final words to Moses are chilling. “Take care never to see my face again.” He sends away the one who has brought him warnings and a way out. The man who says no to God’s messenger has sealed his own fate. Moses’ answer, “You have spoken rightly,” is calm. The time for negotiation is over.

The last plague is announced in 11:4-8, and the tone is grave. Moses speaks “in hot anger” (11:8), but the message is clear and sorrowful: there will be a great cry throughout Egypt such as never was before. God is not delighting in this. It is a judgment on a nation that has killed Israel’s sons (Exodus 1:22) and refused to repent. And in the middle of the announcement is a promise: “The LORD makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel.” You will see tomorrow how.
connection: The darkness of the ninth plague has parallels in the darkness at the cross (Matthew 27:45), when Jesus, the light of the world, bore God’s judgment. Paul writes in Colossians 1:13 that God “has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son.” John 1:5 says, “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it.” Luke 14:33 says, “Any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple.”
application:
Ask yourself where you are bargaining with God. Which parts of your life are you trying to keep out of his reach? It may be your time, your money, your family, or a relationship. Bring that area to him this week.

Thank God that you have light. If you know someone who is in darkness, pray for them, and look for a chance to speak of Christ.

Pray for those who do not know God and who are hardening themselves against him.
prayerPrompts: Confess where you have bargained with God or held something back.
Ask him to take your whole self, your family, and your possessions.
Thank him for bringing you out of darkness into his light.
